paragraphs.source_en: The chronological position of the Kel Essuf engravings in relation to the Bubaline engravings is not certain since they have not been found superimposed. When the rock surface is patinated, the Kel Essuf engravings are always patinated as well. Their position in the relative chronology is established regarding the Round Head paintings which are always found superimposed on these engravings, although the precise length of time between their creations is not established (Fig. 2-6). According to the dark patina and resemblance with the Round Heads in the Acacus, Mori (1967) considers Kel Essuf art to be the earliest anthropomorphic engravings in the Central Sahara from which the Round Head paintings subsequently evolved.

paragraphs.source_en: In 1974 Barich found similar engravings near the excavated shelter of Tin Torha in the Acacus. She attributed these ichthyomorphous symbols to the earliest phases of occupation at the site in the 9th millennium BP when the region experienced very wet climatic conditions (Barich 1974). Striedter, Tauveron and Ferhat (2002-3) postulate a much earlier date for the Kel Essuf. They noticed that in shelters containing Kel Essuf there are also deep kettles on the ground, which are related to ancient water courses. Assuming that the Round Heads superimposed on Kel Essuf were executed in the Early Holocene, the authors postulate the origin of Kel Essuf in earlier times.
